text: EXT.raw_gelu is the C++ function of section 3; any opaque function would do. import torch from torch import Tensor # 1. the operator: namespace::name, the kernel, and what it mutates @torch.library.custom_op( "ext::gelu" , mutates_args=()) def gelu(x: Tensor) -> Tensor: return EXT.raw_gelu(x) # opaque: C++ through pybind11 # 2. the fake: output metadata without running the kernel @gelu.register_fake def _(x): return torch.empty_like(x) # 3. the gradient: its own operator (with its own fake), so compile can trace backward too @torch.library.custom_op( "ext::gelu_bwd" , mutates_args=()) def gelu_bwd(grad: Tensor, x: Tensor) -> Tensor: return EXT.raw_gelu_backward(grad, x) @gelu_bwd.register_fake def _(grad, x): return torch.empty_like(x) def setup_context(ctx, inputs, output): # runs after forward: save what backward needs (x,) = inputs ctx.save_for_backward(x) def backward(ctx, grad): # one gradient per input (x,) = ctx.saved_tensors return gelu_bwd(grad, x) gelu.register_autograd(backward, setup_context=setup_context) # 4. the test torch.library.opcheck(gelu, (torch.randn(4, 8, 32, requires_grad= True ),)) Swapped into every block's MLP ( self.proj(gelu(self.fc(x))) ), the model's loss is , the same as with F.gelu ( ), the largest gradient difference is , and torch.compile(fullgraph=True) gives one graph whose gradients differ from eager by at most measured here, CPU .
